location: Costa Rica (Orosi; Santa Maria de Dota)
finding: Paper covers slope exposure, altitude and yield, not shade. Floral flavour in Orosi depends on slope exposure; chocolate flavour stronger at higher altitude in Dota; taster preference rose with altitude in both; chemical markers correlated weakly with sensory traits
Traditional cultivars: chlorogenic acid and fat rise with elevation; hybrids with Sudanese-Ethiopian ancestry show homeostasis. Ten professional cuppers; composition estimated by NIR calibration
Caffeine, chlorogenic acid and fat rise with elevation; trigonelline and sucrose fall
High altitude and annual rainfall under 1500 mm favoured sensory quality; Olancho and El Paraiso gave the highest-quality coffees
Bean density higher for highland than lowland and midland coffee
Altitude correlated with several bean traits; higher elevation enhanced acidity and flavour complexity; rainfall showed no significant correlation with bean weight, pH, moisture or biochemistry
High altitude with open or medium shade and early-to-mid harvest gave superior quality; authors say the score changes are small
Elevation significant (P<0.05) on screen-14+ retention and most cup variables; high-elevation dry-processed coffees scored raw quality 38.5-40% and cup quality 48.0-51.75% as reported
Title and authors only: effect of altitude on biochemical composition and quality can be affected by shade and processing

Suitability falls at lower Mesoamerican altitudes; higher equatorial South American elevations may gain; Ethiopia and Kenya projected more suitable; India and Vietnam less. Bunn is co-author, not lead.
